newsitem.title: SPAIN: Draft NATO text names Slovenia, Romania for future.
newsitem.headline: Draft NATO text names Slovenia, Romania for future.

text.p: A NATO summit was poised on Tuesday to admit Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary and give a special mention to Slovenia and Romania as deserving cases for future enlargement.
NATO foreign ministers reached a compromise on assurances of an "open door" to be given to former communist states which did not join the first wave of enlargement, delegates said.
The text was still to be approved by heads of state and government when the summit resumed after lunch.

Under the compromise, NATO would identify southeastern Europe and the Baltic region as areas essential to alliance interests without setting a date for admitting states in those regions, the delegates said.
However, a senior French official said NATO would agree formally to review the enlargement process at a 50th anniversary summit in April 1999.

"With regard to the aspiring members, we recognise with great interest and take into account the positive developments towards democracy and the rule of law in a number of southeastern European countries, especially Romania and Slovenia," the draft statement said.

"At the same time, we recognise the progress achieved towards greater stability and cooperation by the states in the Baltic region," it said without specifically naming former Soviet republics Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia to avoid angering Russia, which is adamantly opposed to their joining NATO.

"The Atlantic community recognises its strategic stake in building greater stability, security and regional cooperation in the countries of southeastern Europe and promoting their increasing interests in the Euro-Atlantic community," the proposed document said.
"Progress towards these objectives will be important for our overall goal of a free, prosperous and undivided Europe in peace and will be taken into account in our future accession process," it said.

Seven European allies, led by France and Italy, had urged that Romania and Slovenia be included in the first wave of former communist states to join the Western alliance but the United States and five other allies insisted on restricting the list to three.

Having failed to win a consensus on more than three, the supporters of a broader enlargement sought at least to have the unsuccessful applicants named as prospects for a second wave of expansion, preferably with a commitment to start talks in 1999.
However the United States, facing stiff Congressional resistance to enlargement, was opposed to giving any firm pledge on names or timetables beyond the first three.
